opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's genuinely useful today, but in a specific way. Where models are already pretty good is the scaffolding around kernels: writing the PyTorch reference implementation, the test harness, the benchmarking code, porting a kernel from one framework to another, or explaining what some dense CUDA or Triton code is doing. That's a big chunk of the time a kernel engineer actually spends, so the productivity gain there is real.

When it comes to the hard part, the really performance-critical kernels, it's more mixed. Getting something that's *correct* is increasingly doable. Getting something that's close to hardware peak is a different story. That requires reasoning about memory hierarchy, how you tile things, overlapping data movement with compute, warp specialization, the specifics of the tensor cores on a given generation. A lot of that knowledge isn't well represented in the training data, because there just aren't that many people writing these kernels, and the hardware changes every couple of years. So the models tend to produce code that looks plausible and is maybe 50 or 60 percent of what an expert would get.

What I find most promising is when you put the model in a loop with a verifier. Kernels are a nice domain for that, because you have a clear signal: does it match the reference numerically, and how fast is it? So you can let the model try many variants, profile them, and iterate. That's where I think we'll see fast progress, and some of the recent results on automated kernel generation are encouraging, even if you have to be careful about benchmarks where the model finds shortcuts rather than real speedups.

There's also a role for better abstractions. Part of why we've been working on things like higher-level DSLs for kernels is that if the abstraction is right, both humans and models have an easier time. The model doesn't have to get a thousand low-level details right; it just has to make the few decisions that actually matter for performance.

So my overall view is that it's a strong assistant now, not yet a replacement for an expert on frontier hardware, and the gap is closing faster in this domain than in many others because the feedback is so clean.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because kernel writing is kind of the thing I've spent a big chunk of my life on, and it's honestly changed a lot even in the last year or so.

Where we are right now, I'd say the models are genuinely useful, but useful in a specific way. If you ask a model to write a fused kernel for something that's a fairly standard pattern, like a layer norm, a softmax, an elementwise fusion, a reasonably straightforward reduction, it'll give you something that compiles and is correct a large fraction of the time, and often it's decent. Not state of the art, but decent. For a lot of people that's already a big deal, because historically the barrier to writing any CUDA at all was pretty high. You had to learn the memory hierarchy, how warps work, how to avoid bank conflicts, all that. Now you can get something working in an afternoon that would've taken you a week to learn to write.

Where it gets harder is the stuff that actually matters for performance on modern hardware. If you're on Hopper or Blackwell and you want to hit, say, seventy or eighty percent of peak, you're dealing with things like warp specialization, async memory copies with TMA, the tensor core instruction shapes, pipelining across multiple stages so you're overlapping memory movement with compute. And there the models are less reliable. Part of it is just data. There's not that much public code using those features well, because the hardware is new and the people who know how to do it are a small group. So the model has seen a lot of CUDA from 2015 and not very much from 2024. It'll confidently write something that looks like a Hopper kernel but is actually using the old programming model under the hood.

The other thing I'd point out is that the hard part of kernel engineering was never really typing the code. It's figuring out why your kernel is slow. You profile it, you see you're memory bound when you expected to be compute bound, you have to form a hypothesis about what's going on, maybe there's register spilling, maybe your tile shape is wrong for the occupancy you want. That loop, measure, hypothesize, change, measure again, is where the expertise is. And models today don't do that loop well on their own. They can help you think about it. You paste in the profiler output and ask what's happening and you'll get reasonable suggestions. But closing the loop autonomously, I'd say that's still early.

That said, I'm pretty optimistic about where it's going. A couple reasons. One is that kernels are actually a great target for this kind of thing, because you have an oracle. You can check correctness against a reference implementation, and you can measure speed. So you can set up a search, let the model propose variants, run them, feed back the numbers. We've seen some work along those lines, and I think that's the direction. It stops being "write me a kernel" and becomes "here's a reference, here's a hardware target, go optimize." The other reason is the DSLs are getting better. Triton, and the things built on top of CuTe, ThunderKittens, those raise the level of abstraction so the model has to get fewer low-level details right. A model writing Triton is a lot more likely to produce something good than a model writing raw PTX.

So my honest answer is, today it's a very good assistant for someone who already knows what they're doing, and a very good teacher for someone who doesn't. It's not yet a replacement for the person who knows how to squeeze the last twenty percent out of a new chip. But I think the gap is closing faster than most people in the kernel world expected, and I'd be surprised if in a couple of years a big fraction of the kernels in production weren't at least first drafted by a model.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can write kernels for standard patterns when asked, and that these often compile and are correct, which communicates that it can generate a GPU kernel from a problem description.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re already useful, but there’s a pretty big gap between writing a correct GPU kernel and writing a really fast one. A language model can help you get a first version, explain an API, or translate an operation into Triton. That saves time, especially if you’re working with something unfamiliar.

The hard part is figuring out why a kernel is slow. Are you limited by memory bandwidth? Are you using too many registers? Should you change the tiling, or change the algorithm entirely? The code can look perfectly reasonable and still leave a lot of performance on the table.

So I’m more excited about putting the model in a feedback loop: let it write a kernel, check correctness, benchmark it, look at the results, and iterate. You have a fairly concrete signal there—does it produce the right answer, and how fast is it? Today, I’d treat it as an assistant for someone who can interpret those results. Getting it to make the important optimization decisions reliably is the next step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re useful already, but there’s a big difference between writing a kernel that’s correct and writing one that’s fast. A model can help you get a first implementation, explain an unfamiliar API, or translate between CUDA and Triton. That can save a lot of time.

The harder part is performance. You have to think about memory access, how much work you’re doing per byte you load, register pressure, and how the work maps onto the GPU. A kernel can look perfectly reasonable and still be much slower than an existing implementation.

So I’d treat the model as part of an iterative process: generate something, check correctness, benchmark it, profile it, and use those results to guide the next change. What’s exciting is that kernels give you a fairly concrete feedback signal. You can actually measure whether a proposed change helped. But you still need that measurement loop—you can’t judge performance just by reading the generated code.
